title: Say It, Write It, Share It
bigQuestion: How do you share what you know so others can hear it, and hear what they share back?

story.title: Priya in the Author's Chair
story.kicker: Priya wrote a story. Now she has to read it out loud. Her hands shake a little.
paragraphs: In Priya's class there is a special chair. It is blue. When you sit in it, you are the author. You read your writing. Everyone else listens. Today it is Priya's turn.
Priya sits down. Her paper shakes. She takes a breath. She reads loud and slow. "My little brother lost his shoe at the park. We looked under the slide. We looked in the sand. A dog had it!"
The class laughs at the dog part. Then hands go up. Max asks, "What color was the dog?" Priya says, "Brown, with a white spot." Lily asks, "Did you get the shoe back?" Priya grins. "Yes. It was wet."
Priya stands up. Her hands are not shaking now. Her teacher says, "You read loud and clear. And you answered two good questions." Priya thinks, I might add the wet shoe to my story.
story.think: What did the two questions help Priya think about? What would you ask her?

lessons.title: Listen and Take Turns
lessons.mainIdea: Good talk means one person speaks while the others listen, and then you switch.
reading: Three kids talk at once. "I saw a—" "My dog—" "Wait, listen—" Nobody hears anything. It is just noise. Now one kid talks. The others look at her. They hear every word.
To *listen* means to hear and think about it. Look at the person. Keep your hands still. Wait until they are done. Then it is your turn.
Taking *turns* is like passing a ball. One person has it. Then they pass it. Everyone gets a turn. Nobody grabs. That is how a good talk works.

words.d: to hear what someone says and think about it
your time to talk while others listen

look.title: The Talking Circle
look.text: Look at the rug. Six kids sit in a circle. Rosa holds a small stone. Only the one with the stone talks. She tells about her cat. When she is done, she hands the stone to Deon. Now it is his turn.
look.prompt: Why does the class use a stone? What does it help them do?

check.q: Three kids talk at once. What happens?
check.why: When everyone talks at once, it is just noise. Nobody can hear.

check.q: What does it mean to listen?
choices: To wait with your eyes closed
To hear and think about it
check.why: Listening is hearing what someone says and thinking about it.

check.q: What is taking turns like?
check.why: One person has the turn, then passes it. Everyone gets one.

lessons.title: Ask When You Do Not Know
lessons.mainIdea: If you do not understand, ask a question; it helps you and the speaker.
reading: Mr. Cole says, "Put your work in the bin." Kai does not know which bin. He could guess. He could sit and worry. Or he could ask. "Which bin, Mr. Cole?"
A *question* is how you find out. Asking is smart. It is not a bad thing. Everyone gets confused sometimes. A question fixes it fast.
Good questions start with who, what, where, when, why or how. What do you mean? Where does it go? Can you say it again? Ask, and you will know.

words.d: something you ask to find out what you do not know

look.title: Two Kids, One Direction
look.text: The teacher says, "Get your folder and line up." Nia grabs her folder and goes to the door. Tomas is not sure which folder. He raises his hand. "The red one or the blue one?" The teacher says, "Blue." Now Tomas knows.
look.prompt: What might have happened if Tomas guessed instead of asking?

check.q: Kai does not know which bin. What is the best thing to do?
choices: Put the work in his desk
check.why: A question finds out fast. Asking is smart.

check.q: Which words start good questions?
check.why: Who, what, where, when, why and how are question words.

check.q: Is asking a question a bad thing?
choices: Yes, it means you are not smart
No, it is how you find out
check.why: Everyone gets confused sometimes. Asking is how you fix it.

lessons.title: Loud and Clear
lessons.mainIdea: Speak loud enough to reach the back, slow enough to be understood, and look up.
reading: Ella tells her story to the rug. Her voice is soft. She talks fast. Her hair hides her face. The class leans in. They still miss most of it. Then Ella looks up. She speaks slow and *loud*. Now they hear it all.
To speak loud does not mean to yell. It means your voice reaches the back of the room. To speak *clear* means every word comes out whole. Not mushed together.
Try this. Lift your chin. Look at a face in the back. Say each word. Take a breath at the end of a sentence. Your voice is a gift. Let people have it.

words.d: strong enough to reach across the room, not yelling
easy to understand; every word comes out whole

look.title: Who Heard Ella?
look.prompt: There are 20 kids. Which way of talking reached them all? Why?

check.q: What does speaking loud mean?
choices: Yelling as hard as you can
check.why: Loud means your voice reaches the back of the room. It is not yelling.

check.q: What does clear mean?
choices: Every word is a big word
You do not stop for breath
check.why: Clear means each word is easy to hear and understand.

check.q: Ella's hair hid her face. What should she do?
choices: Lift her chin and look up
check.why: Looking up sends your voice out to the room.

lessons.title: Tell It in Order
lessons.mainIdea: When you tell a story or give directions, say the steps in the order they happen.
reading: Ben tells how to get to the gym. "Turn left. Well, first go out the door. Then, um, past the office." The class is lost. He mixed up the *steps*.
Ben tries again. "First, go out our door. Next, turn left. Then, walk past the office. Last, the gym is on your right." Now everyone can find it.
Stories work the same way. Say what happened first. Then what came next. Then how it ended. Use first, next, then and last. Your listener will follow you.

words.d: the parts of a story or directions, one after another
steps that tell someone how to do something or where to go

look.title: Washing Hands
look.text: Look at the sink. Soap. Water. A towel. Now think of the steps. Turn on the water. Wet your hands. Rub the soap. Rinse. Dry. What if you said dry first, and rub soap last?
look.prompt: Say the hand-washing steps out loud with first, next, then and last.

check.q: Why was the class lost the first time?
check.why: Ben said turn left before go out the door. The order was mixed up.

check.q: What comes last in Ben's directions?
choices: The gym is on your right
check.why: Last, the gym is on your right. That is the end of the directions.

check.q: What words help you tell steps in order?
check.why: First, next, then and last are order words. They show what comes when.

lessons.title: Describe What You See
lessons.mainIdea: To describe a person, place or thing, tell details like size, color, sound and feel.
reading: Guess what I am thinking of. It is a thing. Hard to guess, right? Now listen. It is small. It is round. It is red. It is crunchy. You bite it. An apple!
To *describe* means to tell what something is like. Use details. How big? What color? What sound? How does it feel? What does it smell like?
Describe a person: my grandpa is tall with a gray beard and a soft voice. Describe a place: the library is quiet and smells like paper. Details paint the picture.

words.d: to tell what something is like, using details

look.title: Describe the Bus
look.text: Look at the school bus. It is long and yellow. The door folds open with a hiss. Inside it smells like rubber. The seats are green and bumpy. When it starts, it rumbles under your feet.
look.prompt: Which detail is about a sound? Which one is about a smell?

check.q: What does describe mean?
choices: To tell what something is like
check.why: To describe is to tell what something is like, with details.

check.q: Which one describes an apple best?
choices: It is small, round, red and crunchy.
check.why: Small, round, red and crunchy are details. They help you picture it.

check.q: Which detail tells about a sound?
choices: My grandpa has a soft voice.
check.why: A soft voice is something you hear. Tall is size. Smell is not sound.

lessons.title: Share and Get Feedback
lessons.mainIdea: When you share your writing, listeners can tell you what they liked and what they wonder.
reading: Priya read her story. Max asked about the dog. Lily asked about the shoe. Those questions were *feedback*. They told Priya what her readers wanted to know.
Feedback is what someone tells you about your work. Good feedback says two things. What I liked. What I wonder. I liked the dog part. I wonder what color it was.
When you get feedback, listen. Say thank you. Then think. Should I add that? Priya added the wet shoe. Her story got better because she shared it.

words.d: what someone tells you about your work to help it get better
to read or show your writing to others

look.title: Two Kinds of Feedback
look.text: Max says: I liked when the dog had the shoe. I wonder what the dog looked like. Jo says: It was good. Which feedback helps Priya more?
look.prompt: Why does Max's feedback help more than Jo's?

check.q: What is feedback?
choices: What someone tells you about your work
check.why: Feedback is what a listener tells you to help your work get better.

check.q: Good feedback says what two things?
choices: What I liked and what I wonder
check.why: Tell what you liked. Then tell what you wonder about.

check.q: What did Priya do with her feedback?
check.why: Priya listened and thought. Then she added the wet shoe to her story.

lessons.title: Words That Show Feelings
lessons.mainIdea: Feeling words like proud, scared and excited tell a reader what is inside you.
reading: Jamal said, "I felt proud." Priya said, "My hands shook." Both told a *feeling*. Proud is a feeling word. Shaking hands show a feeling too. Nervous.
There are many feeling words. Happy. Sad. Mad. Scared. Excited. Shy. Proud. Surprised. Each one tells what is going on inside a person.
Add a feeling to your story. I lost my tooth. I felt excited. Or show it. I jumped up and down. Both let the reader feel it with you.

words.d: what is going on inside you, like happy, sad or scared
feeling good about something you did

look.title: Feelings on the Rug
look.prompt: Twenty kids said how they feel before author's chair. Which feeling did the most kids name?

check.q: Which one is a feeling word?
check.why: Scared tells what is going on inside a person. It is a feeling.

check.q: Priya's hands shook. What feeling does that show?
check.why: Shaking hands show a person is nervous.

check.q: How can you show a feeling without naming it?
choices: Tell what your body did, like jumping
check.why: I jumped up and down shows excited without saying the word.

lessons.title: New Words from Books
lessons.mainIdea: Books give you new words; say them, and use them when they fit.
reading: Deon read a book about a fox. The fox was *sly*. Deon did not know that word. He asked. Sly means tricky and clever. Now he had a new word.
Books are full of new words. When you find one, stop. Ask what it means. Say it out loud. Then find a place to use it. My cat is sly. She hides my sock.
Use a new word where it fits. Sly fits a fox or a tricky cat. It does not fit a rock. The more you use a word, the more it is yours.

words.d: a word you did not know before

look.title: A Word from the Story
look.text: Look at Deon's paper. He wrote: The fox was sly. Then he wrote: My little sister is sly. She hid my crayons and smiled. His teacher put a star next to the second one.
look.prompt: Why did the teacher like the second sentence? Where else could sly fit?

check.q: What does sly mean?
check.why: Sly means tricky and clever, like a fox.

check.q: You find a new word in a book. What do you do first?
check.why: Ask what it means. Then say it and use it.

check.q: Where does the word sly fit?
choices: A cat that hides your sock
check.why: A cat that hides things is tricky and clever. That is sly.

review.q: What do you do when someone else is talking?
review.why: Look at the speaker. Wait until they are done. Then it is your turn.

review.q: You do not understand a direction. What should you do?
review.why: Asking is smart. A question finds out fast.
Clear means each word is easy to hear and understand.

choices: Last, walk in. First, open the door.
First, open the door. Then, walk in.
Then, walk in. First, walk in.
review.why: You open the door first, then walk in. First comes before then.

choices: The library is quiet and smells like paper.
review.why: Quiet and smells like paper are details. They tell what the library is like.

review.q: What does good feedback tell a writer?
choices: What I liked and what I wonder
review.why: Good feedback says what you liked and what you wonder about.
